The spacecraft is scheduled to arrive at Phobos in August 2027. Police deployed tear gas and water cannons after protesters - many in masks - threw paving stones, bins and chairs at officers over the weekend. More than 250 people were detained, 80% of whom were minors, Italian police said. The expected crackdown comes after Meloni chaired an emergency security meeting on Monday afternoon. No official announcements have been made. More than 5,000 people gathered in Milan over the weekend. As well as clashes between police and some protesters, stores were looted and property was set on fire. High-end shops in the city's centre closed early on Monday, with many boarding up their windows over fears of further damage. Measures to crack down on youth gangs are expected to be approved as early as Tuesday as part of a decree law, according to Corriere della Sera. Local media reports suggest social media was used to invite young people to Italy's squares over the weekend. Rioting and violence have broken out on the sidelines of mostly peaceful youth-led protests in other European countries including France, Spain and Albania, in recent weeks. Milanese Mayor Giuseppe Sala said he was worried this represented a "new phenomenon" that "originates from an international scenario and therefore feeds itself". Speaking to Ansa, he said he witnessed "smashed shop windows, looted stores, and frightened citizens", adding that "what happened here is what we are seeing in many cities around the world". clusters.text: Nathan Fielder’s secretive Elizabeth Holmes documentary has become a sold-out smash hit and might make Oscars history I f there is one moment that sums up You Can See Everything , the new A24 documentary on Elizabeth Holmes that until this weekend was shrouded in spoiler-averse secrecy, it is, perhaps surprisingly, the one everyone already knows: co-director Nathan Fielder, the droll comedian known for deadpanning subjects into submission, sitting eye to eye with Holmes, the unblinking fabulist of Theranos infamy. In tight zoom, saturation turned up – Fielder’s arched brows and Holmes’s oceanic blue eyes as stark as two magnetic poles – he asks her: “Are you being real right now?” That question hangs over much of the colossal three-hour movie, particularly a claustrophobic first half that has made headlines since the film’s existence was announced in September. That first half – essentially, the only part of the movie anyone respecting spoiler guidelines and/or the theatrical experience could talk about – takes place entirely in 2023, when Fielder and his co-director Lance Oppenheim, along with a small crew, embedded with Holmes, her husband, Billy Evans, and their two small children in the run-up to her prison sentence for fraud. We watch as Fielder, over a few surreal weeks in a beachfront rental, attempts to puncture Holmes’s indomitable facade of faultlessness. It’s not exactly comedic, this chess game between three norms-ignoring people, but it can be quite funny: TV’s grand illusionist, an absurdist auteur who will go as far as actually obtaining a 737 pilot’s license for the bit, stymied by a world-class fabricator, with her poorly dissembling husband on the side. This section resembles, in feel, the pull of an internet wormhole: the closer you zoom in on a subject, without outside context, the more sense devolves. Was Holmes “being real”, for instance, when she told Fielder, with seemingly complete sincerity, that she has never told a lie in her life ? Or when she continued to insist, despite plain reality, that Theranos devices could perform 1,000 diagnostic tests? It’s at once astounding how many people took her seriously, given how obviously mendacious she and her husband appear, and also understandable: the more time you spend with her – the more time you spend watching Fielder spend time with her – the more magnetic the force of her delusions. clusters.text: Can a convict’s right to earn a living weigh as much as a politician’s wish to stand for election? The Allahabad High Court stays murder conviction and life sentence of a Varanasi man while his appeal is pending, and grants him bail. Prayagraj: A man convicted of murder by a Varanasi trial court, who says he wants to contest the 2027 Assembly elections, has had his conviction and life sentence stayed by the Allahabad High Court. He has also been released on bail while his criminal appeal is pending. According to the order, the appeal is yet to be heard and the stay is meant to let him “survive for hearing the final verdict”. The trial court found the allegations proved, but they remain under challenge in appeal, and the High Court has expressed no final view on the merits [Nandlal Rai @ Babloo Rai v. State of U.P.] . On 5 October 2026, a Division Bench of Justice Siddharth and Justice Vinai Kumar Dwivedi passed the order on a bail application in Criminal Appeal No. 1244 of 2026. Advocates Devendra Deo Gupta and P.K. Singh appeared for the appellant. The Additional Government Advocate, for the State, opposed the plea but did not dispute the appellant’s contentions. Reliance was placed by the Bench on the Supreme Court’s decision in Afjal Ansari v. State of U.P. (2024) 2 SCC 187, where convictions of public representatives were stayed because failure to obtain a stay could have irreversible consequences for contesting elections. The Bench then turned to the position of an ordinary convict who is not a legislator, and weighed the two interests against each other: the Court found that the right of a common man to livelihood is not less important than the right of a politician to contest an election. It concluded: the conviction and sentence awarded to the appellant deserves to be stayed during the pendency of this appeal. Bail is on a personal bond and two sureties, and the conviction and sentence stay suspended during the appeal. Without the Court’s leave, the appellant may not transfer, sell or create any charge on his immovable property, and any change of address must be reported within ten days, failing which the State may seek cancellation of bail. Half of the fine, 50 per cent, is to be deposited within one month of release; the other 50 per cent is stayed pending the appeal, and non-payment would lead to recovery in accordance with law.
